newsitem.title: USA: Police say Florida city "not out of the woods yet".
newsitem.headline: Police say Florida city "not out of the woods yet".

text.p: An uneasy calm returned to a poor black neighbourhood on Thursday after a night of shooting and arson set off by a grand jury's decision to clear a white policeman of killing a black youth.

The second bout of racial violence in the city in less than a month was centred near the headquarters of a militant black group that has called for the "execution" of St. Petersburg's mayor and police chief.
The group, already under investigation by federal prosecutors for its role in last month's riot, is part of a national network known as the National People's Democratic Uhuru Movement.
"We don't believe we're out of the woods yet. We've got a continuing crisis in our community," Police Chief Darrel Stephens said.

Stephens and other officials met with the St. Petersburg city council on Thursday in a tense session. One council member, saying she was "furious ... just furious," criticised the police arrests of three members of the Uhuru group Wednesday which inflamed racial tensions in the neighbourhood.

The neighbourhood in south St. Petersburg still smouldered from 103 fires set during the night. Nearly a dozen homes and buildings were destroyed by flames and police used tear gas to disperse groups of angry youths.
Firefighters, fearing gunfire by snipers, let most of the blazes burn themselves out.
Five people were hurt in the melee, including a police officer who was shot in the leg and another in a helicopter who was grazed by a bullet. Three civilians were also treated for gunshot wounds.
The grand jury's action on Wednesday outraged the city's black community, which has complained of being victimised by the police and unable to find decent-paying jobs.

The panel, which included one black member, decided that police officer James Knight was justified in shooting Tyron Lewis, 18, the night of Oct. 24. The jury said that Knight was in danger of being run over by Lewis' car when the officer fired three times, striking Lewis in the heart and arm.
Last month's shooting set off a night of rioting in which 11 people were hurt and 30 businesses and homes set ablaze.

Leaders of the Coalition of African American Leadership, a moderate group, said on Thursday they were considering a variety of measures to protest the police and grand jury actions including an economic boycott, a civil lawsuit against police and peaceful marches outside city hall.
A federal civil rights investigation of last month's police shooting is already under way separate from the grand jury's investigation.

The Uhuru group, named after a Swahili word for "freedom," recently called for the execution of St. Petersburg's police chief and mayor after conducting its own trial. The group has about 100 members and is led by Joe Waller, a former member of the Black Panthers who took the name Omali Yeshitela, according to Raymond Arsenault, a University of South Florida professor who has studied the group.

"We've had threats, constant threats for the past two weeks, saying that if the report from the grand jury didn't meet with their satisfaction that the town was going to burn," Stephens told reporters.
The group is part of a national network with chapters in Oakland, California, and Chicago and was founded in 1991.

Three members of the Uhuru group were arrested on Wednesday afternoon for minor traffic offences to get them off the streets, police said. A crowd gathered at the Uhuru headquarters after police arrested one man and officers clashed with other group members.
Shortly after the grand jury decision, the group handed out flyers for an evening meeting that urged black citizens to organise against being "shot down in the streets like dogs."

Although Knight was cleared by the grand jury, the police department suspended him for 60 days without pay for failing to follow correct procedures. The department said Knight had not done enough to get himself out of danger before firing.
